cells.tense: The first clean sight of this is arriving now, and you are tending it while it grows.
cells.act: read the hardest page of it twice, slowly, before you stop
cells.ask: Take the hardest part of what you're tending — the page you'd skip — and read it twice, slow, without moving on. Going all the way into it is the work; you'll meet the edge of it there.
cells.core:
What you're tending is beginning to show itself, and you have the patience for the early stage of it. Nothing is forced. You watch it come up, you give it what a young thing needs, and it stays clear because you aren't asking it to be finished yet.

The depth is available to you now. Take one piece of what you're growing and go further into it than feels comfortable — until you meet the edge of it. Read the hardest part twice, slow, without moving on. The pattern underneath will open on the second pass. That's what this moment asks: not more care, a deeper look. The care and the depth aren't separate jobs.

cells.tense: You are already finishing what is only just beginning to grow, and bracing for how it will land.
cells.act: carry what the spark became to its full size
cells.ask: Pick the smallest thing you've begun in what you're tending. Carry it only to its next natural step, not the finished version — then leave it there a while and push no further.
cells.core:
You can see what it's going to become, and that picture is running past the growing. The end is being built in your head while the thing itself is still small. You're carrying it forward before it's ready to be carried, and the care is starting to feel like managing an outcome.

Come back to the size it actually is right now. Take the smallest thing you've begun in what you're tending and carry it only to its next natural step — not the finished version — then leave it there a while and push no further. Meeting what's here, not the version you're already imagining, is the whole work. The spark can burn without you walking it to the end on the same day.
cells.sheetLine: You see the end of it before it has finished growing.
cells.verb: catching the first clean cut of what's actually there
cells.place: the ground where you tend what's still growing and not yet finished

cells.tense: You were tending something and you are still standing at a door that is already behind you.
cells.act: complete the form so it stands without you
cells.ask: Instead of tending harder this week, finish something: pick one piece of care you've already given, nearly done, and bring it to where it holds up by itself. One thing, not the whole garden.
cells.core:
The care has gone quiet. You were tending something, and somewhere in it you stopped arriving — still going through the motions, not really there. What was growing is still there, and the hand that tended it has pulled back. The first clear sight you had of it is a memory now, not a practice.

Don't try to feel your way back into the care. Finish something instead. Pick one piece of care you've already given — something nearly done — and bring it to where it holds up by itself this week. Not the whole garden; one thing. Finishing one piece by sustained will pulls the current back through the care. It returns through the hands, not through pushing feeling into the place that's gone quiet.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped arriving, and the care went quiet.

cells.tense: You are already opening the next door in what you tend, and you'd call it keeping up.
cells.act: open the door to the next thing on time, not early
cells.ask: When something in what you tend asks to move on this week, open that door on time — not early, not sooner. Let one thing change stage on the day it changes, and know it was your hand.
cells.core:
What you're tending keeps moving into its next stage, and you keep it moving. You'd say you're just keeping up with it, or doing what it needs. The eye that catches the first sign of change in it, the hand that opens the next door — that's yours, and your account leaves you out.

When something in what you tend asks to move on this week, open that door on time — not early, not sooner. Let one thing change stage on the day it changes, and know it was your hand that did it. Noticing arrives first, and noticing is the door. That's the turn: the moment a thing changes isn't fate, it's what you caught and met.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim: 'the first clear seeing has arrived and hasn't yet cut anything' reads into what they are about to perceive, which the record does not give me. The reader's objection: 'I'm not beginning to see anything — I'm just tending what's already growing,' especially at Unacknowledged, where I assert authorship they may reasonably deny. The asks all survive being wrong — tending, carrying a start to its finish, finishing a piece of the care itself, opening the door to what's next are useful acts regardless of whether my read of the perception is correct. The sentence that serves me more than them is anything about 'a new clarity dawns' — it flatters the card and tells the person nothing they can hold.
